question: A wave on a string has speed \(30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) when produced at \(5.0\,\text{Hz}\). The same string under the same tension is driven at \(10\,\text{Hz}\). The new wavelength is
explanation:
\( \textbf{String condition:} \) The same string and same tension mean the wave speed remains \(30\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{New frequency:} \)
\[
f'=10\,\text{Hz}=10\,\text{s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) New wavelength \(\lambda'\).
\( \textbf{Wave relation:} \)
\[
v=f'\lambda'
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
\lambda'=\frac{v}{f'}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda'=\frac{30\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{10\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda'=3.0\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new wavelength is \(3.0\,\text{m}\).
The frequency has changed, but the speed remains fixed because the string conditions are unchanged.

question: The derivation of \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\) for a stretched string mainly depends on the idea that
opt_a: tension supplies the restoring force for a small string element
opt_b: the string particles move permanently along the string with the wave
opt_c: the wave speed is fixed only by the frequency of the oscillator
opt_d: gravity must be the only force acting on every element of the string
explanation: In the usual derivation for a wave on a stretched string, a small element of the string is considered. When the string is slightly curved by a transverse disturbance, the tensions at the two ends of the small element have components that provide a restoring force. This restoring force produces transverse acceleration of the string element. The inertia involved is measured by the mass per unit length, \(\mu\). Combining the restoring effect of tension with the inertia of the string gives \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). The derivation is based on small transverse disturbances, not on permanent transport of string material.

question: A dimensional check is applied to \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). Since \(T_s\) has unit \(\text{N}\) and \(\mu\) has unit \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\), the unit of \(\frac{T_s}{\mu}\) is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Tension unit:} \)
\[
\text{N}=\text{kg m s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Linear mass density unit:} \)
\[
\mu=\text{kg m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Ratio unit:} \)
\[
\frac{T_s}{\mu}=\frac{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}{\text{kg m}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Canceling \(\text{kg}\):} \)
\[
\frac{T_s}{\mu}=\text{m s}^{-2}\times\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\frac{T_s}{\mu}=\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Taking square root:} \)
\[
\sqrt{\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}}=\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The unit of \(\frac{T_s}{\mu}\) is \(\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\).
The square root then correctly gives the unit of wave speed.

question: The formula \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\) is used for a stretched string most safely when the wave is
opt_a: a small transverse disturbance on a uniform string
opt_b: a sound wave travelling through vacuum
opt_c: a large permanent flow of string material
opt_d: a wave whose speed is controlled only by amplitude
explanation: The standard string-wave formula assumes a stretched string with uniform linear mass density. The disturbance is treated as small so that the string tension remains nearly constant and the usual small-slope approximation is valid. The wave is transverse because the string elements move perpendicular to the direction of propagation. The formula is not for sound in vacuum, because sound needs a medium and the string formula uses string tension and linear density. It is also not a formula for bulk motion of string material. The physical conditions behind the relation matter as much as the algebraic form.

question: A string of length \(2.0\,\text{m}\) has mass \(0.040\,\text{kg}\). It is stretched with tension \(80\,\text{N}\). The transverse wave speed on the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Length \(L=2.0\,\text{m}\), mass \(m=0.040\,\text{kg}\), tension \(T_s=80\,\text{N}\).
\( \textbf{First find linear mass density:} \)
\[
\mu=\frac{m}{L}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution for \(\mu\):} \)
\[
\mu=\frac{0.040\,\text{kg}}{2.0\,\text{m}}=0.020\,\text{kg m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Wave speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{80}{0.020}}
\]
\( \textbf{Intermediate value:} \)
\[
\frac{80}{0.020}=4000
\]
\( \textbf{Square root:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{4000}\approx63\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is approximately \(63\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The mass must first be converted into mass per unit length before using the string-speed formula.

question: A musician wants to double the wave speed on a string without changing the string itself. The required change in tension is
explanation:
\( \textbf{String unchanged:} \) The linear mass density \(\mu\) remains constant.
\( \textbf{Speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Required condition:} \)
\[
v'=2v
\]
\( \textbf{Using proportionality:} \)
\[
v\propto\sqrt{T_s}
\]
\( \textbf{Ratio form:} \)
\[
\frac{v'}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{T_s'}{T_s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
2=\sqrt{\frac{T_s'}{T_s}}
\]
\( \textbf{Squaring:} \)
\[
4=\frac{T_s'}{T_s}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension must be made four times.
Doubling speed requires quadrupling tension because the relation contains a square root.

question:
The following statements refer to transverse waves on stretched strings.
I. Increasing \(T_s\) increases wave speed if \(\mu\) is constant.
II. Increasing \(\mu\) increases wave speed if \(T_s\) is constant.
III. In the same string under the same tension, changing frequency changes wavelength rather than wave speed.
The supported statements are
explanation: Statement I is supported by \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\), because increasing \(T_s\) increases the speed. Statement II is not supported because increasing \(\mu\) increases inertia per unit length and decreases speed. Statement III is supported because, in the same string under the same tension, \(T_s\) and \(\mu\) remain unchanged. The speed therefore remains fixed while the relation \(v=f\lambda\) makes wavelength adjust when frequency changes. This is a common place where source-controlled frequency and medium-controlled speed must be kept separate. The correct set keeps both the formula and the physical meaning consistent.

question: Two strings have the same length and are under the same tension. String R is made of a denser material, so its mass per unit length is larger. A pulse sent along string R will travel
opt_a: faster than on the lighter string
opt_b: slower than on the lighter string
opt_c: with the same speed regardless of mass per unit length
opt_d: only if the source frequency is zero
explanation: The speed of a transverse pulse on a stretched string is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). The two strings have the same tension, so the difference comes from \(\mu\). A denser or heavier string has larger mass per unit length. Larger \(\mu\) means more inertia must be accelerated by the restoring force due to tension. Therefore, the wave speed is smaller on the heavier string. The pulse can still travel, but it travels more slowly because the string has more inertia per unit length.

question: A graph is plotted between \(v^2\) and \(T_s\) for transverse waves on a string of fixed linear mass density \(\mu\). The graph is a straight line through the origin. Its slope is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Starting relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Squaring both sides:} \)
\[
v^2=\frac{T_s}{\mu}
\]
\( \textbf{Writing in graph form:} \)
\[
v^2=\left(\frac{1}{\mu}\right)T_s
\]
\( \textbf{Comparison with straight-line form:} \) If \(v^2\) is plotted on the vertical axis and \(T_s\) on the horizontal axis, the slope is \(\frac{1}{\mu}\).
\( \textbf{Intercept:} \) The ideal relation passes through the origin.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The slope is \(\frac{1}{\mu}\).
This graph form removes the square root and makes the inverse dependence on linear mass density visible.

question: A string has \(\mu=0.025\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\). The measured slope of a \(v^2\) versus \(T_s\) graph should be
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Linear mass density \(\mu=0.025\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Graph relation:} \)
\[
v^2=\left(\frac{1}{\mu}\right)T_s
\]
\( \textbf{Slope of \(v^2\) versus \(T_s\):} \)
\[
\text{slope}=\frac{1}{\mu}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\text{slope}=\frac{1}{0.025\,\text{kg m}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\text{slope}=40\,\text{kg}^{-1}\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Unit check:} \) Since \(\frac{v^2}{T_s}=\frac{\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}}{\text{kg m s}^{-2}}=\text{kg}^{-1}\text{m}\), the unit is consistent.
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The slope is \(40\,\text{kg}^{-1}\text{m}\).
The slope is the reciprocal of \(\mu\), not \(\mu\) itself.

question: Linear mass density \(\mu\) of a string is defined as
explanation: Linear mass density tells how much mass is present per unit length of a string. If a string has mass \(m\) and length \(L\), then \(\mu=\frac{m}{L}\). Its SI unit is \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\). This quantity is important because a string with larger \(\mu\) has greater inertia per unit length. In the wave-speed relation \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\), larger \(\mu\) gives smaller speed for the same tension. The reciprocal \(\frac{L}{m}\) would describe length per unit mass, not mass per unit length.

question: A string of length \(5.0\,\text{m}\) has total mass \(0.10\,\text{kg}\). Its linear mass density is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Mass \(m=0.10\,\text{kg}\), length \(L=5.0\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Linear mass density \(\mu\).
\( \textbf{Definition:} \)
\[
\mu=\frac{m}{L}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\mu=\frac{0.10\,\text{kg}}{5.0\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\mu=0.020\,\text{kg m}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The linear mass density is \(0.020\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).
The unit must be mass per length, so \(\text{kg m}^{-1}\) confirms the correct ratio.

question: A string is made thicker using the same material and is kept under the same tension as before. For transverse waves on the string, the speed is expected to
opt_a: increase because the string is thicker
opt_b: decrease because linear mass density is larger
opt_c: remain unchanged because the material is the same
explanation: The speed of a transverse wave on a stretched string is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). If the same material is made into a thicker string, the mass per unit length \(\mu\) increases. With the same tension \(T_s\), a larger \(\mu\) gives a smaller value of \(\frac{T_s}{\mu}\). Therefore, the wave speed decreases. The material being the same does not mean the linear mass density is unchanged, because thickness affects mass per unit length. The physical reason is that a heavier string has more inertia for the same restoring tension.

question: A transverse wave travels at \(50\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) on a string of linear mass density \(0.020\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\). The tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Wave speed \(v=50\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), linear mass density \(\mu=0.020\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Tension \(T_s\).
\( \textbf{String-wave relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Squaring both sides:} \)
\[
v^2=\frac{T_s}{\mu}
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
T_s=\mu v^2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
T_s=(0.020)(50)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
(50)^2=2500
\]
\[
T_s=0.020\times2500=50\,\text{N}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The string tension is \(50\,\text{N}\).
The speed must be squared before multiplying by \(\mu\).

question: Two equal-length strings are stretched with the same tension. String P has mass \(0.050\,\text{kg}\), and string Q has mass \(0.200\,\text{kg}\). The speed of waves on Q compared with P is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Same length condition:} \) For equal lengths, linear mass density is proportional to total mass.
\( \textbf{Mass ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{\mu_Q}{\mu_P}=\frac{0.200}{0.050}=4
\]
\( \textbf{Same tension relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Speed ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\sqrt{\frac{\mu_P}{\mu_Q}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\frac{1}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed on string Q is one-half the speed on string P.
The fourfold increase in mass per unit length gives a twofold decrease in speed because of the square root.

question: A record for a stretched string says: \(m=0.060\,\text{kg}\), \(L=3.0\,\text{m}\), and \(T_s=45\,\text{N}\). The correct sequence for finding the wave speed is
explanation: The string-speed formula uses linear mass density \(\mu\), not total mass \(m\) directly. Therefore, the first step is to calculate \(\mu=\frac{m}{L}\). After that, the wave speed is found from \(v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}\). Using \(m\) in place of \(\mu\) would ignore the length of the string and give a wrong unit. Removing the square root would also make the result dimensionally wrong for speed. The formula connects restoring tension with inertia per unit length, so both \(T_s\) and \(\mu\) must be used in their correct roles.

question: A sound wave cannot travel through a perfect vacuum because
opt_a: no particles pass on pressure disturbances
opt_b: its wavelength becomes larger than any possible distance
opt_c: its frequency must become exactly zero
opt_d: electromagnetic waves block sound waves in vacuum
explanation: Sound is a mechanical wave, so it needs a material medium for propagation. In air, sound travels through compressions and rarefactions of air particles. A perfect vacuum has no particles that can be compressed or rarefied. Without particles, there is no mechanism to pass the disturbance from one region to another. The frequency of the source may still exist as vibration of the source, but the sound wave cannot propagate through the vacuum. This separates sound from electromagnetic waves such as light, which can travel through vacuum.

question: The speed of sound in a material medium depends mainly on
opt_a: the colour of the medium and the shape of the source
opt_b: the distance from the listener only
opt_c: the loudness of the sound only
opt_d: the elasticity of the medium and its inertia
explanation: Sound travels because the medium can be compressed and then restore itself. The elastic property of the medium provides the restoring effect. The density or inertia of the medium resists rapid motion of its particles. Sound speed depends on the balance between these two features. A medium with strong restoring ability and relatively low inertia tends to transmit sound faster. Loudness and distance affect the received intensity, but they do not by themselves define the basic speed of sound in the medium.

question: Sound generally travels faster in solids than in gases because solids usually have
explanation: Sound propagation requires neighbouring particles of the medium to interact and pass on a disturbance. Solids generally have particles that are strongly connected, so a disturbance can be transmitted rapidly. Although solids may have high density, their elastic restoring forces are usually much stronger than those in gases. This often makes sound speed greater in solids than in liquids and gases. A gas has weaker elastic restoring response under ordinary conditions. The speed comparison depends on both elasticity and inertia, not on density alone.

question: A bell rings inside a closed jar. As air is gradually removed, the sound heard outside becomes weaker, although the bell is still seen vibrating. This observation shows that
opt_a: sound needs a material medium for propagation
opt_b: light needs air more than sound does
opt_c: the bell stops vibrating immediately in vacuum
explanation: The vibrating bell acts as the source of the sound. When air is present, air particles carry the pressure disturbance from the bell to the outside. As air is removed, fewer particles are available to transmit the disturbance, so the sound becomes weaker. The bell may still be visible because light can travel through the glass and evacuated region. This contrast shows that sound is mechanical, while light is electromagnetic. The decreasing sound is therefore due to removal of the medium, not due to disappearance of the source vibration.

explanation: Sound is a mechanical disturbance, so it needs a material medium. Row Q is suitable because particles of the medium interact and pass on compressions and rarefactions. Row P is not suitable because a perfect vacuum has no particles to carry sound. Row R is also unsuitable because absence of particles does not make sound infinitely fast; it prevents sound propagation. Row S is not suitable because sound does not become electromagnetic just because light is present. The correct idea is that sound propagation requires matter.

question: Two media are compared for sound propagation. Medium P has a stronger elastic restoring effect but similar inertia compared with medium Q. The sound speed in P is expected to be
opt_a: smaller because stronger elasticity resists all motion
opt_b: zero because elastic media cannot carry sound
opt_d: larger because stronger elasticity raises wave speed
explanation: Sound travels by the repeated compression and restoration of the medium. A stronger elastic restoring effect helps a compressed region return and pass the disturbance onward more rapidly. If the inertia is similar, the medium with greater elasticity generally gives a greater sound speed. Elasticity does not prevent wave motion; it supplies the restoring influence needed for wave propagation. Inertia also matters because heavier medium particles resist acceleration. The comparison keeps inertia similar, so the stronger restoring effect is the deciding factor.

question: A gas and a solid are both able to transmit sound. The main reason both can do so is that both
opt_a: have particles that interact with neighbours
opt_d: transport their entire mass permanently with the sound
explanation: Sound needs a material medium whose particles can pass on a disturbance. In a gas, particles transmit sound through pressure and density variations. In a solid, particles transmit sound through elastic interactions with neighbouring particles. The microscopic details differ, but both media contain matter capable of carrying mechanical disturbances. The medium does not need to move permanently from source to listener. Sound energy is transferred through local motion and interaction of particles.

question:
Assertion: Sound cannot be heard across a perfect vacuum.
Reason: Sound is a mechanical wave that needs a material medium to carry pressure disturbances.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true because a perfect vacuum has no material particles to transmit sound. Sound in ordinary media travels through pressure and density changes. The Reason is also true because sound is a mechanical wave and requires a material medium. Without a medium, there can be no chain of compressions and rarefactions reaching the listener. The Reason directly explains why sound cannot be heard across a perfect vacuum. Source vibration alone is not enough; a transmitting medium is also required.

question: A sound wave travels from air into water. The frequency of the sound is fixed by the vibrating source. If the speed of sound is greater in water than in air, the wavelength in water is
opt_c: unchanged because wavelength is fixed by the source only
explanation: The source fixes the frequency of the sound. When sound enters another medium, the speed can change because medium properties are different. The relation \(v=f\lambda\) still connects speed, frequency, and wavelength. If \(v\) increases while \(f\) stays unchanged, \(\lambda\) must increase. The wavelength is therefore larger in water under the stated condition. This is the same adjustment principle used for waves crossing from one medium to another.

question: A sound wave of frequency \(500\,\text{Hz}\) travels in air with speed \(340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Its wavelength in air is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Frequency \(f=500\,\text{Hz}=500\,\text{s}^{-1}\), sound speed \(v=340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wavelength \(\lambda\).
\( \textbf{Wave relation:} \)
\[
v=f\lambda
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
\lambda=\frac{v}{f}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda=\frac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{500\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda=0.68\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength is \(0.68\,\text{m}\).
The speed of sound is divided by frequency because wavelength is the distance travelled in one cycle.

question: A statement says, “Sound travels faster in a medium only because its particles are closer together.” The better view is that sound speed depends on
explanation: Particle spacing can influence how a medium behaves, but it is not the only factor deciding sound speed. Sound speed depends on how strongly the medium restores itself after compression and how much inertia resists motion. Elasticity provides the restoring effect, while density or inertia affects how rapidly the particles can accelerate. A solid often transmits sound quickly because its elastic response is strong. A dense medium does not automatically give faster sound if the restoring effect is not also considered. The reliable description uses elasticity and inertia together.

question: A sound wave travels through a medium where particles are difficult to compress but also have large inertia. A careful prediction of sound speed should consider
opt_d: neither property because sound speed is source-controlled
explanation: Difficulty of compression is connected with the medium’s elastic response. A stronger elastic response tends to increase sound speed because the disturbance is restored and passed on more quickly. Large inertia tends to reduce speed because more mass resists acceleration. The actual speed depends on the balance of these effects. The source sets the frequency of the sound, but it does not alone decide the propagation speed in a given medium. A careful prediction must therefore include both elasticity and inertia.

question: In a basic comparison of sound speeds, the usual order for many materials is
opt_a: gases faster than liquids faster than solids
opt_b: solids faster than liquids faster than gases
opt_c: liquids faster than solids faster than gases
opt_d: vacuum faster than solids faster than gases
explanation: In many common materials, sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. This general trend occurs because solids usually have much stronger elastic restoring forces than liquids and gases. Liquids are generally less rigid than solids but still transmit sound better than gases. Gases have relatively weak elastic response under ordinary conditions, so sound is often slowest in gases. The order is a broad rule and not a substitute for using actual material data when given. Vacuum is not included as a fastest medium because sound cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum.

RowWaveVacuum propagationBasic type

explanation: Light is an electromagnetic wave and can propagate through vacuum, so row Q is suitable. Sound is a mechanical wave and cannot propagate through a perfect vacuum, so row R is suitable. Row P is unsuitable because it says sound can propagate in vacuum. Row S is unsuitable because it classifies light as mechanical and says it cannot propagate in vacuum. The comparison is based on whether a material medium is required. Sound needs matter to carry pressure disturbances, while light does not.

question: The speed of a longitudinal wave in a fluid is related to bulk modulus \(B\) and density \(\rho\) by
explanation: In a fluid, sound or any small longitudinal pressure disturbance travels because the fluid has elasticity and inertia. The bulk modulus \(B\) measures the resistance of the fluid to compression, so it provides the restoring effect. Density \(\rho\) represents inertia per unit volume, which resists rapid motion of the fluid elements. The speed is therefore larger when \(B\) is larger and smaller when \(\rho\) is larger. The formula \(v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\) expresses this balance. The square root is essential because the ratio \(\frac{B}{\rho}\) has the dimensions of speed squared.

question: A liquid has bulk modulus \(B=2.0\times10^9\,\text{Pa}\) and density \(\rho=1.0\times10^3\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\). The speed of a longitudinal wave in it is closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Bulk modulus \(B=2.0\times10^9\,\text{Pa}\), density \(\rho=1.0\times10^3\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Longitudinal wave speed \(v\).
\( \textbf{Relation for a fluid:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{2.0\times10^9}{1.0\times10^3}}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplifying the ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{2.0\times10^9}{1.0\times10^3}=2.0\times10^6
\]
\( \textbf{Taking square root:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{2.0\times10^6}
\]
\[
v\approx1.4\times10^3\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wave speed is closest to \(1.4\times10^3\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Using \(\frac{B}{\rho}\) without the square root would give a quantity with unit \(\text{m}^2\text{s}^{-2}\), not speed.

question: A dimensional check is made for the relation \(v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\). The quantity \(\frac{B}{\rho}\) has the dimensions of
explanation:
\( \textbf{Bulk modulus dimension:} \) Bulk modulus has the same dimension as pressure.
\[
[B]=[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]
\]
\( \textbf{Density dimension:} \)
\[
[\rho]=[ML^{-3}]
\]
\( \textbf{Ratio dimension:} \)
\[
\left[\frac{B}{\rho}\right]=\frac{[ML^{-1}T^{-2}]}{[ML^{-3}]}
\]
\( \textbf{Canceling \(M\):} \)
\[
\left[\frac{B}{\rho}\right]=L^{2}T^{-2}
\]
\( \textbf{Interpretation:} \)
\[
[L^{2}T^{-2}]=[\text{speed}]^2
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(\frac{B}{\rho}\) has the dimensions of speed squared.
That is why the square root in \(v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\) produces the dimension of speed.

question: Two fluids have the same bulk modulus. Fluid Q has four times the density of fluid P. If the speed of sound in P is \(v\), the speed in Q is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Speed relation in a fluid:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}
\]
\( \textbf{Same bulk modulus condition:} \) \(B_Q=B_P=B\).
\( \textbf{Density relation:} \)
\[
\rho_Q=4\rho_P
\]
\( \textbf{Speed in P:} \)
\[
v_P=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho_P}}=v
\]
\( \textbf{Speed in Q:} \)
\[
v_Q=\sqrt{\frac{B}{4\rho_P}}
\]
\( \textbf{Taking out the factor:} \)
\[
v_Q=\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho_P}}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed in Q is \(\frac{v}{2}\).
A fourfold increase in density gives a twofold decrease in speed because density appears under the square root.

question: Newton’s formula for the speed of sound in a gas used \(v=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\rho}}\). Its main limitation is that it assumes the pressure changes are
opt_a: isothermal, so the predicted speed is too low
opt_b: adiabatic, giving exactly the observed speed in every gas
opt_c: electromagnetic, so no gas particles are needed
opt_d: independent of pressure and density separately
explanation: Newton treated the compressions and rarefactions of sound in a gas as if they occurred isothermally. In an isothermal change, heat exchange keeps temperature constant, so the effective elastic response is too small for rapid sound propagation. Sound compressions and rarefactions occur very quickly, so there is not enough time for heat exchange between neighbouring layers. Newton’s formula \(v=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\rho}}\) therefore predicts a speed lower than the observed speed in air. Laplace corrected this by treating the changes as adiabatic. The limitation is not that sound is non-mechanical; it is the thermodynamic assumption used for gas compression.

question:
Study the table and identify the row that properly compares Newton’s and Laplace’s treatment of sound in a gas.
RowTreatmentFormula idea
PNewton: isothermal change\(v=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\rho}}\)
QLaplace: adiabatic change\(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\)
RNewton: no material medium\(v=\sqrt{\frac{B}{\rho}}\)
SLaplace: electromagnetic wave in gas\(v=f\lambda\) only
The fully suitable pair of rows is
explanation: Newton’s treatment used an isothermal assumption for gas compression and led to \(v=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\rho}}\), so row P is suitable. Laplace recognized that sound compressions and rarefactions are rapid and nearly adiabatic, leading to \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\), so row Q is suitable. Row R is unsuitable because Newton did not treat sound as propagation without a medium. Row S is unsuitable because Laplace’s correction is still about a mechanical sound wave in a gas. The factor \(\gamma\) appears because the gas compression is adiabatic rather than isothermal.

question: Laplace’s correction changes Newton’s sound-speed formula in a gas mainly by replacing \(P\) with
explanation: Newton’s formula for sound speed in a gas was \(v=\sqrt{\frac{P}{\rho}}\). Laplace corrected it by treating the pressure and density variations in sound as adiabatic. For an adiabatic change, the effective bulk modulus of the gas becomes \(\gamma P\), where \(\gamma\) is the ratio of specific heats. Therefore, the corrected formula is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\). The correction increases the predicted speed because \(\gamma\gt1\) for ordinary gases. The factor belongs inside the square root as part of the gas’s effective elastic response.

question: Air has pressure \(P=1.0\times10^5\,\text{Pa}\), density \(\rho=1.25\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), and \(\gamma=1.4\). The speed of sound using Laplace’s formula is closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(P=1.0\times10^5\,\text{Pa}\), \(\rho=1.25\,\text{kg m}^{-3}\), \(\gamma=1.4\).
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Speed of sound \(v\).
\( \textbf{Laplace formula:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{(1.4)(1.0\times10^5)}{1.25}}
\]
\( \textbf{Numerator:} \)
\[
(1.4)(1.0\times10^5)=1.4\times10^5
\]
\( \textbf{Division:} \)
\[
\frac{1.4\times10^5}{1.25}=1.12\times10^5
\]
\( \textbf{Square root:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{1.12\times10^5}\approx335\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed of sound is approximately \(335\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
Using Newton’s formula without \(\gamma\) would give a smaller value.

question: For an ideal gas, the speed of sound may be written as \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}\). At the same temperature and with the same \(\gamma\), the gas with smaller molar mass \(M\) has
explanation: In the ideal-gas expression \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}\), \(\gamma\), \(R\), and \(T\) are kept the same in the comparison. The only changing quantity is molar mass \(M\). Since \(M\) is in the denominator under the square root, smaller \(M\) gives larger \(\frac{\gamma RT}{M}\). Therefore, lighter gases generally transmit sound faster under the stated conditions. This is why sound travels faster in helium than in a much heavier gas at the same temperature, if the other factors are comparable. The dependence is inverse-square-root, not direct inverse.

question: In an ideal gas, the absolute temperature changes from \(T\) to \(4T\), while the gas type remains the same. The speed of sound changes from \(v\) to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Temperature dependence:} \)
\[
v\propto\sqrt{T}
\]
\( \textbf{Initial temperature:} \) \(T\), with speed \(v\).
\( \textbf{New temperature:} \)
\[
T'=4T
\]
\( \textbf{Speed ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{v'}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{T'}{T}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{v'}{v}=\sqrt{\frac{4T}{T}}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\frac{v'}{v}=2
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The speed becomes \(2v\).
The temperature must be taken on the absolute Kelvin scale in this proportionality.

question: The speed of sound in a gas is \(340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) at \(300\,\text{K}\). If the same gas is heated to \(400\,\text{K}\), the new speed is closest to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(v_1=340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), \(T_1=300\,\text{K}\), \(T_2=400\,\text{K}\).
\( \textbf{Temperature relation:} \)
\[
v\propto\sqrt{T}
\]
\( \textbf{Ratio form:} \)
\[
\frac{v_2}{v_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_2}{T_1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v_2=340\sqrt{\frac{400}{300}}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplifying the ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{400}{300}=\frac{4}{3}
\]
\( \textbf{Square root:} \)
\[
\sqrt{\frac{4}{3}}\approx1.155
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v_2\approx340(1.155)\approx393\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new speed is closest to \(393\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
The Celsius scale cannot be used directly in the square-root temperature ratio.

question: For an ideal gas at fixed temperature, increasing the pressure does not change the sound speed if the gas remains ideal. The reason is that
opt_a: pressure and density increase in the same ratio
opt_b: pressure increases but density must become zero
opt_c: sound speed is always independent of temperature
opt_d: pressure alone fixes sound speed while density has no role
explanation: For an ideal gas, the sound speed can be written as \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\). At fixed temperature for a given gas, the ideal gas relation makes \(\frac{P}{\rho}\) equal to \(\frac{RT}{M}\). If pressure is increased at fixed temperature, density increases in the same ratio. Therefore, the ratio \(\frac{P}{\rho}\) remains unchanged. Since \(\gamma\) is also unchanged for the same gas, the sound speed remains unchanged. This pressure independence applies under the stated ideal-gas and fixed-temperature conditions.

question:
Use the graph description below.
For the same ideal gas, a graph is drawn with sound speed \(v\) on the vertical axis and \(\sqrt{T}\) on the horizontal axis, where \(T\) is absolute temperature.
The graph should be
opt_b: a horizontal line for all temperatures
opt_d: a straight line through the origin
explanation: For the same ideal gas, \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}\). The constants \(\gamma\), \(R\), and \(M\) are unchanged for the same gas. Therefore, \(v\propto\sqrt{T}\). If \(v\) is plotted against \(\sqrt{T}\), the relation has the form \(y=mx\). This gives a straight line through the origin in the idealized relation. A graph of \(v\) against \(T\) would not be a straight line of this same type because of the square-root dependence. The graph only has this simple form when \(T\) is measured in Kelvin.

question: A gas at \(300\,\text{K}\) is compressed so that its pressure doubles, while its temperature is kept constant and ideal-gas behaviour is assumed. The speed of sound in the gas
explanation: In an ideal gas, sound speed is \(v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma P}{\rho}}\). At fixed temperature for the same gas, pressure and density are proportional to each other. If pressure doubles, density also doubles. The ratio \(\frac{P}{\rho}\) therefore remains the same. Since \(\gamma\) is unchanged, the sound speed remains unchanged. The pressure change alone would not decide the speed unless the accompanying density and temperature conditions were also specified.

question: Two ideal gases have the same \(\gamma\) and are at the same temperature. Gas P has molar mass \(M\), while gas Q has molar mass \(4M\). If the sound speed in P is \(v\), the sound speed in Q is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Ideal-gas sound speed:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{\gamma RT}{M}}
\]
\( \textbf{Same quantities:} \) \(\gamma\), \(R\), and \(T\) are the same for the two gases.
\( \textbf{Molar mass relation:} \)
\[
M_Q=4M_P
\]
\( \textbf{Speed ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\sqrt{\frac{M_P}{M_Q}}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\sqrt{\frac{M_P}{4M_P}}
\]
\( \textbf{Simplification:} \)
\[
\frac{v_Q}{v_P}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{1}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The sound speed in Q is \(\frac{v}{2}\).
A fourfold increase in molar mass gives a twofold decrease in speed because \(M\) is under the square root.

question: A sound wave in air is represented by pressure variation and displacement variation. At a compression, the pressure variation is
explanation: A compression is a region where air particles are closer together than in the undisturbed state. This crowding means density is higher than normal. The pressure is also higher than normal, so the pressure variation is positive. In a sinusoidal pressure representation, a compression corresponds to a pressure maximum. A rarefaction corresponds to a pressure minimum or maximum negative pressure variation. The pressure description should not be confused with the displacement graph of individual air particles.

question: In a longitudinal sound wave, displacement and pressure variations are not the same graph. The particle displacement is zero at the centre of a compression because nearby particles are
opt_a: displaced away from that centre from both sides
opt_b: moving only perpendicular to the wave direction
opt_d: displaced toward that centre from both sides
explanation: In a compression, particles are crowded together around that region. On one side of the compression centre, particles are displaced toward the centre from the left. On the other side, particles are displaced toward the centre from the right. At the centre itself, the displacement changes sign, so the displacement may be zero even though pressure is maximum. This shows why pressure and displacement variations are not in the same phase in a sound wave. A pressure maximum does not mean a maximum particle displacement at the same position.

question:
Study the table for a longitudinal sound wave and identify the mismatched row.
RowRegionPressure and density condition
PCompressionPressure higher than normal
QRarefactionDensity lower than normal
RCompressionParticles closer together
SRarefactionPressure higher than normal
explanation: A rarefaction is a region where particles are farther apart than normal. Its density is lower than normal, and its pressure is also lower than normal. Row S is therefore mismatched because it assigns higher pressure to a rarefaction. Row P is suitable because a compression has pressure higher than normal. Row Q is suitable because a rarefaction has density lower than normal. Row R is suitable because a compression is a crowded region of the medium. Pressure and density rise together in compressions and fall together in rarefactions.

question: In a plane sound wave, the pressure variation is related to the particle displacement \(s\) by the spatial change of \(s\). A suitable local relation is
explanation: Pressure variation in a longitudinal wave is connected with compression or expansion of the medium. Compression is produced when nearby particles are displaced toward each other, and this is measured by the spatial gradient \(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\). The bulk modulus \(B\) connects pressure change with fractional volume change. The negative sign appears because a negative displacement gradient corresponds to compression and hence positive pressure variation. A time derivative would describe particle velocity, not the pressure variation itself. The pressure pattern depends on how displacement changes from place to place, not merely on the displacement value at one point.

question: A longitudinal sound wave has displacement \(s=s_0\sin(kx-\omega t)\). The pressure variation is proportional to
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given displacement:} \)
\[
s=s_0\sin(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Pressure-displacement relation:} \)
\[
\Delta p=-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}
\]
\( \textbf{Differentiate with respect to \(x\):} \)
\[
\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}=ks_0\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Substitute into pressure relation:} \)
\[
\Delta p=-Bks_0\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Proportionality:} \)
\[
\Delta p\propto-\cos(kx-\omega t)
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The pressure variation is proportional to \(-\cos(kx-\omega t)\).
The pressure variation is \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) out of phase with the displacement variation because it depends on the spatial gradient of displacement.

question:
Use the graph description below.
Two graphs are drawn for the same longitudinal sound wave at the same instant. Graph P shows particle displacement \(s\) versus \(x\). Graph Q shows pressure variation \(\Delta p\) versus \(x\).
At a position where \(s\) is maximum positive in Graph P, Graph Q has
opt_d: pressure variation equal to the wave speed
explanation: In a longitudinal sound wave, pressure variation is related to the spatial gradient of particle displacement. At a maximum or minimum of the displacement graph, the local slope \(\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\) is zero. Since \(\Delta p=-B\frac{\partial s}{\partial x}\), the pressure variation is zero at a displacement maximum. A pressure maximum occurs where displacement crosses zero with a suitable slope. This is why the displacement and pressure graphs are not in phase. Reading a displacement crest as a pressure compression would mix two different wave representations.

question: In a sound wave, a pressure maximum and a displacement maximum do not occur at the same position because
opt_a: pressure variation depends on displacement gradient
opt_b: pressure variation depends only on the source frequency
opt_c: displacement is absent in longitudinal waves
opt_d: sound waves are transverse inside gases
explanation: A sound wave in a gas is longitudinal, so particles do have displacement along the direction of propagation. The pressure variation is not determined only by the displacement value at a point. It depends on whether neighbouring particles are crowding together or spreading apart. That crowding is measured by the spatial gradient of displacement. A displacement maximum has zero local slope, so it does not correspond to a pressure maximum. A compression occurs where the displacement pattern makes particles converge toward a region.

question:
Study the table for a sinusoidal sound wave and identify the mismatched row.
RowDisplacement conditionPressure condition
PDisplacement maximumPressure variation zero
QDisplacement minimumPressure variation zero
RDisplacement zero with particles convergingCompression
SDisplacement maximumCompression always
explanation: Row S is mismatched because a displacement maximum does not automatically mean a compression. At a displacement maximum, the slope of the displacement graph is zero, so the pressure variation is zero in the sinusoidal description. A compression occurs where particles converge, which corresponds to a suitable zero crossing of displacement with non-zero gradient. Rows P and Q are suitable because both displacement extremes have zero pressure variation. Row R is suitable because convergence of neighbouring particles creates a pressure and density maximum. The pressure pattern must be inferred from particle crowding, not from displacement height alone.

question: The principle of superposition for small waves says that when two waves overlap, the resultant displacement is
opt_a: the product of their individual displacements
opt_c: always equal to the larger displacement only
opt_d: always zero when the waves overlap completely
explanation: For small disturbances in a linear medium, the principle of superposition applies. If two waves arrive at the same point at the same time, the resultant displacement is \(y=y_1+y_2\). The addition is algebraic, so signs and directions of displacement matter. Two upward displacements reinforce, while an upward and a downward displacement partly or completely cancel. The waves do not permanently destroy each other during overlap. After passing through each other in a linear medium, each wave continues with its own identity.

question: Two pulses on a string overlap at a point. At that instant, pulse P gives displacement \(+3.0\,\text{cm}\), and pulse Q gives displacement \(-1.5\,\text{cm}\). The resultant displacement at that point is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given displacements:} \) \(y_1=+3.0\,\text{cm}\), \(y_2=-1.5\,\text{cm}\).
\( \textbf{Principle used:} \)
\[
y=y_1+y_2
\]
This relation applies because overlapping displacements add algebraically in a linear medium.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
y=(+3.0\,\text{cm})+(-1.5\,\text{cm})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
y=+1.5\,\text{cm}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant displacement is \(+1.5\,\text{cm}\).
Adding magnitudes without signs would incorrectly treat opposite displacements as reinforcing.

question: Two identical upward pulses meet on a string. At the instant of complete overlap, the displacement of the string is
opt_a: unchanged from one pulse because waves cannot add
opt_d: reversed in direction because reflection occurs
explanation: When two identical upward pulses overlap, their displacements at corresponding points have the same sign. By superposition, the resultant displacement is the algebraic sum of the two displacements. Since the pulses are identical and both upward, the maximum displacement during complete overlap becomes twice that of one pulse. This is constructive interference. The pulses are not reflected merely because they meet each other on the string. In the linear wave model, they pass through after overlap and regain their separate shapes.

question: Two equal pulses on a string approach each other, one upward and one downward. At the instant they exactly overlap, the string is momentarily straight. The best interpretation is that
opt_a: the two pulses permanently lose their energy at overlap
opt_b: the wave speed becomes zero everywhere after overlap
opt_c: the string becomes unable to carry waves after overlap
opt_d: resultant displacement is zero by destructive interference
explanation: An upward pulse and an equal downward pulse have displacements of equal magnitude and opposite sign at corresponding points. When they exactly overlap, algebraic addition gives zero resultant displacement. This is destructive interference in displacement. The pulses have not permanently disappeared; in a linear medium, they continue moving after overlap. Energy is not judged only by the instantaneous shape of the string at one moment. The straight-string instant shows cancellation of displacement, not permanent removal of the waves.

question:
Assertion: Two overlapping small-amplitude waves can pass through each other without permanently changing their shapes.
Reason: In a linear medium, the resultant displacement during overlap is the algebraic sum of the individual displacements.
opt_a: Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason explains Assertion
opt_b: Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason does not explain Assertion
opt_c: Assertion is true, but Reason is false
opt_d: Assertion is false, but Reason is true
explanation: The Assertion is true for small waves in a linear medium. During overlap, the medium displacement is obtained by adding the individual wave displacements. This addition produces a temporary resultant shape, such as reinforcement or cancellation. The individual waves are not treated as permanent objects that collide and deform each other. After overlap, each wave continues as if it had passed through the other. The Reason gives the mathematical basis for that temporary-overlap behaviour.

question:
The following statements refer to interference of two waves at a point.
I. Constructive interference occurs when displacements are in the same direction.
II. Destructive interference occurs when displacements are in opposite directions.
III. Superposition means adding wave speeds at the point of overlap.
The supported statements are
explanation: Constructive interference occurs when the overlapping wave displacements reinforce each other. Destructive interference occurs when the overlapping displacements oppose each other. These ideas come from algebraic addition of displacement. Statement III is not supported because superposition adds displacements, not wave speeds. Wave speed is a property of propagation through the medium, while displacement is the local disturbance being added. Keeping these quantities separate prevents confusion between interference and propagation.

question: Two waves of the same amplitude \(A\) reach a point in phase. A third case has the same two waves reaching the point with phase difference \(\pi\). The resultant amplitudes in the two cases are respectively
explanation:
\( \textbf{Case 1:} \) The two waves reach the point in phase.
\( \textbf{In-phase result:} \) Their displacements have the same sign at every corresponding instant, so the amplitudes add.
\[
A_{\text{result}}=A+A=2A
\]
\( \textbf{Case 2:} \) The phase difference is \(\pi\).
\( \textbf{Opposite-phase result:} \) The displacements are equal in magnitude and opposite in sign.
\[
A_{\text{result}}=A-A=0
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The resultant amplitudes are \(2A\) and \(0\).
The phase relation decides whether equal amplitudes reinforce or cancel.

question: A pulse travelling along a string reaches a rigid wall where the end of the string is fixed. The reflected pulse is
opt_a: not inverted, with no phase change
opt_b: converted completely into a longitudinal sound wave
opt_c: stopped permanently at the wall with no reflection
opt_d: inverted, with a phase change of \(\pi\)
explanation: At a fixed end, the end point of the string cannot move. The incident and reflected disturbances must combine so that the displacement at the fixed end remains zero. This condition is satisfied when the reflected pulse is inverted relative to the incident pulse. In sinusoidal language, this corresponds to a phase change of \(\pi\). The reflected wave still travels back along the string, but with displacement reversed. The fixed boundary behaves as a displacement node.

question:
Use the arrangement described below.
A pulse travelling along a string reaches a ring that can slide freely on a frictionless vertical rod. The ring marks the end of the string, but it is free to move up and down.
The reflected pulse from this end is
opt_a: inverted because the end is fixed
opt_b: not inverted because the end is free to move
opt_c: always destroyed because the rod is frictionless
opt_d: changed into a wave of zero frequency
explanation: A free end can move with the disturbance, so it does not force the displacement at the end to be zero. Because the end is not fixed, the reflected pulse does not need to invert to satisfy a zero-displacement boundary condition. The free end behaves like a displacement antinode in the related standing-wave picture. The pulse is reflected, but its displacement direction is not reversed. The frictionless rod allows vertical motion of the ring, which is exactly the condition that distinguishes this end from a rigidly fixed end.

question: A pulse reflects from a fixed end of a string. If the incident pulse has an upward displacement near the end, the reflected pulse near the end has
opt_b: no displacement anywhere on the string
opt_d: displacement only along the string length
explanation: Reflection at a fixed end produces inversion of the pulse. An upward incident displacement reflects as a downward displacement. This reversal is needed because the fixed end itself must remain at zero displacement. The incident and reflected waves superpose near the boundary to satisfy that condition. The reflected pulse is not absent; it travels back along the string with reversed sign. Direction of propagation changes along the string, while the transverse displacement sign is inverted.

question: A wave pulse goes from a light string to a heavier string joined at a boundary. Part of the pulse is reflected and part is transmitted. The frequency of the transmitted wave is
opt_a: the same as the incident wave frequency
opt_b: always double the incident wave frequency
opt_c: always half the incident wave frequency
opt_d: zero because a boundary is crossed
explanation: At a boundary between two media, the source continues to decide the frequency of the disturbance. The transmitted wave must match the timing of the oscillations arriving at the boundary. The speed can change in the second string because the medium properties are different. Since \(v=f\lambda\), a change in speed is accompanied by a change in wavelength when \(f\) remains fixed. The boundary can divide energy into reflected and transmitted parts, but it does not create a new source frequency. Frequency continuity at the boundary is a key idea for waves crossing media.

question: A transverse pulse travels from a lighter string into a heavier string joined at a boundary. The reflected pulse in the lighter string is usually
opt_a: not inverted because the heavier string has no inertia
opt_b: absent because all energy must pass into the heavier string
opt_c: converted into a sound wave in air
opt_d: inverted, like reflection from a fixed end
explanation: When a pulse on a lighter string reaches a heavier string, the boundary offers greater inertia to the incoming disturbance. Part of the wave is transmitted into the heavier string and part is reflected back into the lighter string. The reflected pulse is inverted, similar to reflection from a fixed end, though the boundary is not perfectly fixed. The transmitted pulse continues into the heavier string with a different speed. Frequency remains fixed by the incoming disturbance at the boundary. The inversion is a boundary-condition effect, not a destruction of the incident pulse.

question: A pulse travelling on a heavier string reaches a junction with a lighter string. The reflected pulse in the heavier string is generally
opt_d: changed into a standing wave immediately
explanation: Reflection at a boundary depends on the relative wave impedance or effective inertia of the two strings. When a pulse travels from a heavier string to a lighter string, the boundary is more like a free end than a fixed end. The reflected pulse is therefore not inverted. Part of the disturbance is transmitted into the lighter string, where the wave speed is different. The boundary does not force the displacement to be zero as a rigid fixed end would. The sign of the reflected pulse is decided by how the junction responds to the incident disturbance.

question: A pulse on a string reaches a boundary between two strings. The incident, reflected, and transmitted pulses are observed. The quantity that must remain the same for the reflected and transmitted waves as compared with the incident wave is
explanation: The frequency is fixed by the rate at which the incident disturbance reaches the boundary. The boundary must oscillate with the same time pattern, so the reflected and transmitted waves have the same frequency as the incident wave. The wave speed may change in the second string because the medium properties are different. Since \(v=f\lambda\), wavelength can change when speed changes while frequency remains the same. Amplitude also depends on how energy is divided at the boundary. The time rhythm is continuous across the boundary, while spatial spacing adjusts to the medium.

question: A wave of frequency \(20\,\text{Hz}\) travels from string P, where its speed is \(8.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), into string Q, where its speed is \(4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). The wavelength in string Q is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Frequency \(f=20\,\text{Hz}=20\,\text{s}^{-1}\), speed in string Q \(v_Q=4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Boundary idea:} \) The frequency remains unchanged when the wave crosses the junction.
\( \textbf{Required quantity:} \) Wavelength in string Q, \(\lambda_Q\).
\( \textbf{Wave relation:} \)
\[
v_Q=f\lambda_Q
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging:} \)
\[
\lambda_Q=\frac{v_Q}{f}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda_Q=\frac{4.0\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{20\,\text{s}^{-1}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda_Q=0.20\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength in string Q is \(0.20\,\text{m}\).
The speed from string P is not used for the wavelength inside string Q.

question:
Study the table for pulse reflection at boundaries and identify the mismatched row.
RowBoundary situationReflected pulse
PFixed endInverted
QFree endNot inverted
RLight string to heavier stringUsually inverted
SHeavy string to lighter stringAlways inverted like a fixed end
explanation: A fixed end reflects a pulse with inversion, so row P is suitable. A free end reflects a pulse without inversion, so row Q is suitable. A pulse going from a lighter string toward a heavier string is reflected with inversion because the boundary behaves partly like a fixed end. A pulse going from a heavier string toward a lighter string is generally reflected without inversion, so row S is mismatched. The transmitted pulse still enters the second string in both string-junction cases. The sign of reflection is linked to the boundary response, not merely to the fact that reflection occurs.

question: Two identical waves of the same amplitude and frequency travel along the same string in opposite directions. Their superposition can form
opt_b: a single pulse moving faster than both waves
opt_c: a wave with no nodes possible
opt_d: a permanent flow of string material
explanation: A standing wave is formed by the superposition of two waves of the same frequency, same amplitude, and same speed travelling in opposite directions. The resulting pattern does not travel along the string as a whole. Instead, it has fixed points of zero displacement called nodes and points of maximum oscillation called antinodes. Energy is not carried along the string in the same way as in a single progressive wave. The particles between nodes oscillate with different amplitudes. The fixed pattern comes from continuous interference of the two opposite travelling waves.

question: In a standing wave on a string, a node is a point where
explanation: A node is a fixed point in a standing wave pattern where the resultant displacement remains zero at all times. This happens because the two opposite travelling waves always cancel at that point. The string may have large motion at nearby points, but the node itself stays at rest. An antinode is the point where the displacement amplitude is maximum. The existence of a node does not mean the wave has zero frequency; the whole pattern still oscillates with the source frequency. Nodes are positions of permanent destructive interference in the standing wave.

question: In a standing wave, an antinode is best described as a point where
opt_b: the displacement is zero at every instant
opt_c: the string is cut into two separate pieces
opt_d: the wave changes from transverse to longitudinal
explanation: An antinode is a point in a standing wave where the amplitude of oscillation is maximum. The displacement at an antinode changes with time, becoming maximum positive, zero, and maximum negative during a cycle. It is not a point that stays permanently at maximum displacement. A node, not an antinode, remains at zero displacement at all times. Antinodes occur midway between neighbouring nodes in the simplest standing-wave pattern. The word maximum refers to amplitude of oscillation, not to a constant displacement value.

question: The distance between two neighbouring nodes in a standing wave is
explanation: In a standing wave, nodes are points of permanent destructive interference. The pattern repeats from one node to the next after half a wavelength. Therefore, the separation between two neighbouring nodes is \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\). The same separation also occurs between two neighbouring antinodes. A node and the nearest antinode are separated by \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\). The full wavelength contains two node-to-node intervals in the standing-wave pattern.

question: A node and the nearest antinode in a standing wave on a string are separated by \(0.15\,\text{m}\). The wavelength of the waves forming the standing wave is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Distance between a node and the nearest antinode \(=0.15\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Standing-wave spacing rule:} \)
\[
\text{node to nearest antinode}=\frac{\lambda}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\frac{\lambda}{4}=0.15\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Solving for wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda=4(0.15\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda=0.60\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength is \(0.60\,\text{m}\).
Using \(0.15\,\text{m}\) as the whole wavelength would confuse a quarter-pattern spacing with a full spatial cycle.

question:
Use the arrangement described below.
A string is fixed at both ends and vibrates in a standing-wave pattern. The simplest pattern has one loop between the fixed ends.
For this simplest pattern, the length \(L\) of the string is related to wavelength by
explanation: A fixed end of a string must be a node because it cannot move. In the simplest standing-wave pattern on a string fixed at both ends, there is one loop with nodes at the two ends and one antinode in the middle. The distance between neighbouring nodes is \(\frac{\lambda}{2}\). Since the two fixed ends are neighbouring nodes in the fundamental pattern, the string length is \(L=\frac{\lambda}{2}\). This means the fundamental wavelength is \(\lambda=2L\). The one-loop pattern is the lowest-frequency mode of the fixed string.

question: A string fixed at both ends has length \(1.2\,\text{m}\). In its fundamental mode, the wavelength is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Length of string \(L=1.2\,\text{m}\).
\( \textbf{Fundamental mode condition:} \) For a string fixed at both ends, the simplest standing-wave pattern has
\[
L=\frac{\lambda}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Solving for wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda=2L
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda=2(1.2\,\text{m})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda=2.4\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The fundamental wavelength is \(2.4\,\text{m}\).
The string length is half of the wavelength in the fundamental mode, not the full wavelength.

question: For a string fixed at both ends, the allowed wavelengths are
explanation:
A string fixed at both ends must have nodes at both ends. An allowed standing wave must fit an integral number of half-wavelengths into the string length. Therefore,
\[
L=n\frac{\lambda_n}{2}
\]
where \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\). Solving for \(\lambda_n\) gives \(\lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n}\). The first mode has \(\lambda_1=2L\), the second has \(\lambda_2=L\), and so on. The condition comes from boundary nodes, not from an arbitrary choice of wavelength.

question: The frequency of the \(n\)-th harmonic of a string fixed at both ends is
explanation:
For a string fixed at both ends, the allowed wavelengths are \(\lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n}\). The wave relation is \(v=f_n\lambda_n\). Therefore,
\[
f_n=\frac{v}{\lambda_n}
\]
Substituting \(\lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n}\) gives
\[
f_n=\frac{v}{2L/n}
\]
\[
f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}
\]
The frequencies are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency \(f_1=\frac{v}{2L}\). This harmonic series occurs because both ends are fixed nodes.

question: A string fixed at both ends has length \(0.80\,\text{m}\), and the wave speed on it is \(160\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Its fundamental frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) String length \(L=0.80\,\text{m}\), wave speed \(v=160\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Fundamental frequency relation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{v}{2L}
\]
This relation applies because the fundamental mode has \(\lambda_1=2L\).
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{160\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{2(0.80\,\text{m})}
\]
\( \textbf{Denominator:} \)
\[
2(0.80)=1.60\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{160}{1.60}=100\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The fundamental frequency is \(100\,\text{Hz}\).
The factor \(2L\) appears because the fundamental wavelength is twice the string length.

question: A string fixed at both ends has fundamental frequency \(60\,\text{Hz}\). The frequency of its third harmonic is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Fundamental frequency \(f_1=60\,\text{Hz}\).
\( \textbf{Harmonic relation for a fixed string:} \)
\[
f_n=n f_1
\]
\( \textbf{For the third harmonic:} \)
\[
n=3
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f_3=3(60\,\text{Hz})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f_3=180\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The third harmonic has frequency \(180\,\text{Hz}\).
For a string fixed at both ends, all integral harmonics are allowed in the ideal model.

question: A fixed string vibrates in a mode with three loops between its ends. This mode corresponds to
explanation: In a string fixed at both ends, each loop represents one half-wavelength segment. The number of loops in the standing-wave pattern equals the harmonic number \(n\). One loop is the first harmonic, two loops give the second harmonic, and three loops give the third harmonic. The ends remain nodes in every mode. The wavelength for three loops is \(\lambda=\frac{2L}{3}\). Counting loops is a direct visual way to identify the harmonic number for a fixed string.

question: A string fixed at both ends is vibrating in the second harmonic. The number of nodes and antinodes present along the string, including the end nodes, is
explanation: The second harmonic of a string fixed at both ends has two loops. Each loop contains one antinode, so there are \(2\) antinodes. The fixed ends are nodes, and there is one additional node between the two loops. Therefore, the total number of nodes is \(3\). In general, for the \(n\)-th harmonic of a fixed string, there are \(n\) antinodes and \(n+1\) nodes. The end nodes must be included because the string is fixed at both ends.

question: A string fixed at both ends is vibrating in its third harmonic. Including the fixed ends, the number of nodes and antinodes is
explanation: For a string fixed at both ends, the \(n\)-th harmonic has \(n\) loops. Each loop contains one antinode, so the third harmonic has \(3\) antinodes. The fixed ends are nodes, and there are additional nodes between adjacent loops. In general, the \(n\)-th harmonic has \(n+1\) nodes when the end nodes are included. For \(n=3\), the number of nodes is \(4\). The count follows from the standing-wave shape, not from the frequency value alone.

question: A string of length \(1.0\,\text{m}\) is fixed at both ends and vibrates in the fourth harmonic. The wavelength of the standing wave pattern is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) String length \(L=1.0\,\text{m}\), harmonic number \(n=4\).
\( \textbf{Allowed wavelength relation:} \)
\[
\lambda_n=\frac{2L}{n}
\]
This relation applies because a string fixed at both ends must contain an integral number of half-wavelengths.
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
\lambda_4=\frac{2(1.0\,\text{m})}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
\lambda_4=0.50\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The wavelength in the fourth harmonic is \(0.50\,\text{m}\).
Four loops fit into the string, so each loop has length \(\frac{\lambda}{2}=0.25\,\text{m}\).

question: A string fixed at both ends has fundamental frequency \(80\,\text{Hz}\). If the tension is made four times while \(L\) and \(\mu\) remain unchanged, the new fundamental frequency becomes
explanation:
\( \textbf{Original fundamental frequency:} \) \(f_1=80\,\text{Hz}\).
\( \textbf{String frequency relation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{1}{2L}\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Quantities kept fixed:} \) \(L\) and \(\mu\) are unchanged.
\( \textbf{Proportionality:} \)
\[
f_1\propto\sqrt{T_s}
\]
\( \textbf{New tension:} \)
\[
T_s'=4T_s
\]
\( \textbf{Frequency ratio:} \)
\[
\frac{f_1'}{f_1}=\sqrt{\frac{T_s'}{T_s}}=\sqrt{4}=2
\]
\( \textbf{New frequency:} \)
\[
f_1'=2(80\,\text{Hz})=160\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The new fundamental frequency is \(160\,\text{Hz}\).
The frequency doubles because the wave speed doubles when the tension is made four times.

explanation: For a string fixed at both ends, the frequencies are integral multiples of the fundamental frequency. Therefore, \(f_n=nf_1\), so the fourth harmonic has \(f_4=4f_1\), not \(\frac{f_1}{4}\). Row P is suitable because the fundamental mode has \(L=\frac{\lambda_1}{2}\), giving \(\lambda_1=2L\). Row Q is suitable because \(\lambda_2=\frac{2L}{2}=L\). Row R is suitable because \(f_3=3f_1\). The mismatched row reverses the harmonic-frequency relation.

question: A graph is plotted for a fixed string with harmonic number \(n\) on the horizontal axis and allowed frequency \(f_n\) on the vertical axis. If the wave speed on the string is constant, the graph is
opt_a: a straight line through the origin
opt_b: a rectangular hyperbola through the origin
opt_d: a horizontal line through every harmonic
explanation: For a string fixed at both ends, the allowed frequencies are given by \(f_n=\frac{nv}{2L}\). If \(v\) and \(L\) are fixed, then \(f_n\) is directly proportional to \(n\). This has the straight-line form \(f_n=\left(\frac{v}{2L}\right)n\). The graph passes through the origin in the ideal mathematical relation. Its slope is \(\frac{v}{2L}\), which is the fundamental frequency \(f_1\). A hyperbola would suggest inverse dependence, but the harmonic frequencies increase linearly with harmonic number.

question: A string of length \(0.50\,\text{m}\) and linear mass density \(0.010\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\) is fixed at both ends. Its fundamental frequency is \(100\,\text{Hz}\). The tension in the string is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) \(L=0.50\,\text{m}\), \(\mu=0.010\,\text{kg m}^{-1}\), \(f_1=100\,\text{Hz}\).
\( \textbf{Fundamental frequency relation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{v}{2L}
\]
\( \textbf{Finding wave speed:} \)
\[
v=2Lf_1
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
v=2(0.50\,\text{m})(100\,\text{s}^{-1})
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
v=100\,\text{m s}^{-1}
\]
\( \textbf{String-speed relation:} \)
\[
v=\sqrt{\frac{T_s}{\mu}}
\]
\( \textbf{Rearranging for tension:} \)
\[
T_s=\mu v^2
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
T_s=(0.010)(100)^2
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The tension is \(100\,\text{N}\).
The frequency condition first fixes the wave speed, and the string formula then fixes the required tension.

question: A claim says, “A string fixed at both ends can vibrate only in odd harmonics.” The best correction is that
opt_a: a fixed string ideally supports all integral harmonics
opt_b: a fixed string supports no harmonics because both ends are nodes
opt_c: a fixed string supports only the fundamental frequency
opt_d: a fixed string supports only even harmonics
explanation: A string fixed at both ends must have nodes at both ends. This boundary condition is satisfied when the length contains \(n\) half-wavelengths, where \(n=1,2,3,\ldots\). Therefore, the allowed frequencies are \(f_n=nf_1\). This includes both odd and even harmonics. The second harmonic, for example, has two loops and a node at the middle in addition to the end nodes. The “odd harmonics only” rule belongs to a different boundary condition, such as a pipe closed at one end and open at the other.

question: In a standing sound wave inside a pipe, a closed end is usually treated as
opt_a: a displacement antinode and pressure node
opt_b: both displacement node and pressure node
opt_c: both displacement antinode and pressure antinode
opt_d: a displacement node and pressure antinode
explanation: At a closed end of an air column, the air layer next to the wall cannot move freely along the pipe. Therefore, the particle displacement is zero there, making it a displacement node. However, the pressure variation is maximum near the closed end because compression and rarefaction are strongest at that boundary. This makes the closed end a pressure antinode. Displacement and pressure standing-wave patterns are shifted relative to each other in a sound wave. The boundary condition must be applied to particle motion, not only to pressure.

question: At an open end of a pipe supporting a standing sound wave, the usual boundary condition is
opt_d: no relation to displacement or pressure
explanation: At an open end of a pipe, air particles can move relatively freely. This makes the open end approximately a displacement antinode. The pressure variation at the open end is close to atmospheric pressure, so the pressure variation is approximately zero there. Therefore, the open end is treated as a pressure node. This is opposite to the closed end, where displacement is zero but pressure variation is maximum. Remembering both descriptions prevents mixing up displacement and pressure patterns in air columns.

question: A pipe open at both ends vibrates in its fundamental mode. The length \(L\) of the pipe is related to the wavelength by
explanation: In a pipe open at both ends, both ends are displacement antinodes. In the fundamental mode, the simplest standing-wave pattern has one node between the two open ends. The distance from one displacement antinode to the next antinode in this pattern is half a wavelength. Therefore, \(L=\frac{\lambda}{2}\). This gives \(\lambda=2L\), the same fundamental wavelength relation as a string fixed at both ends. The boundary types differ, but the half-wavelength fitting condition is the same for the fundamental mode.

question: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other vibrates in its fundamental mode. The length \(L\) of the air column is
explanation: A pipe closed at one end has a displacement node at the closed end. The open end is a displacement antinode. The shortest standing-wave pattern that satisfies these two boundary conditions is one quarter of a wavelength. Therefore, \(L=\frac{\lambda}{4}\) in the fundamental mode. This means \(\lambda=4L\). The closed-open pipe differs from an open-open pipe because its two ends require different displacement conditions.

question: An open pipe of length \(0.85\,\text{m}\) has sound speed \(340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\). Its fundamental frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Pipe length \(L=0.85\,\text{m}\), sound speed \(v=340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Open-open fundamental condition:} \)
\[
L=\frac{\lambda_1}{2}
\]
\( \textbf{Fundamental wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda_1=2L=2(0.85\,\text{m})=1.70\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Frequency relation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{v}{\lambda_1}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{1.70\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f_1=200\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The fundamental frequency is \(200\,\text{Hz}\).
The open pipe contains half a wavelength in its fundamental mode.

question: A pipe closed at one end has length \(0.85\,\text{m}\). If the speed of sound is \(340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\), its fundamental frequency is
explanation:
\( \textbf{Given data:} \) Pipe length \(L=0.85\,\text{m}\), sound speed \(v=340\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).
\( \textbf{Closed-open fundamental condition:} \)
\[
L=\frac{\lambda_1}{4}
\]
\( \textbf{Fundamental wavelength:} \)
\[
\lambda_1=4L=4(0.85\,\text{m})=3.40\,\text{m}
\]
\( \textbf{Frequency relation:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{v}{\lambda_1}
\]
\( \textbf{Substitution:} \)
\[
f_1=\frac{340\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{3.40\,\text{m}}
\]
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f_1=100\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The fundamental frequency is \(100\,\text{Hz}\).
For the same length, a closed-open pipe has twice the fundamental wavelength of an open-open pipe.

question: Two pipes have the same length and contain air at the same temperature. Pipe P is open at both ends, while pipe Q is closed at one end. Their fundamental frequencies satisfy
explanation:
For an open-open pipe, the fundamental frequency is \(f_P=\frac{v}{2L}\). For a closed-open pipe, the fundamental frequency is \(f_Q=\frac{v}{4L}\). The two pipes have the same length and the same sound speed because the air conditions are the same. Therefore,
\[
\frac{f_P}{f_Q}=\frac{v/(2L)}{v/(4L)}
\]
\[
\frac{f_P}{f_Q}=2
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) \(f_P=2f_Q\).
The open-open pipe has a shorter fundamental wavelength, so its fundamental frequency is higher.

question: The allowed harmonics of an ideal pipe closed at one end and open at the other are
explanation: A closed-open pipe must have a displacement node at the closed end and a displacement antinode at the open end. The allowed standing-wave patterns contain an odd number of quarter-wavelength segments. Therefore, the allowed frequencies are \(f_1, 3f_1, 5f_1,\ldots\). Even harmonics do not satisfy the node-antinode boundary condition at the two ends. This is different from a string fixed at both ends or a pipe open at both ends, where all integral harmonics are allowed. The missing even harmonics come from the unequal boundary conditions.

question: A closed pipe has fundamental frequency \(120\,\text{Hz}\). The next higher resonant frequency is
explanation:

\( \textbf{Allowed series for a closed-open pipe:} \)
\[
f_1,\;3f_1,\;5f_1,\ldots
\]
The next higher resonance after the fundamental is the third harmonic.
\( \textbf{Calculation:} \)
\[
f_3=3f_1=3(120\,\text{Hz})
\]
\[
f_3=360\,\text{Hz}
\]
\( \textbf{Final answer:} \) The next higher resonant frequency is \(360\,\text{Hz}\).
The frequency \(240\,\text{Hz}\) would be the second harmonic, which is not allowed in an ideal closed-open pipe.

question:
Use the arrangement described below.
An air column has one end closed by a piston and the other end open to air. In the fundamental resonance, the closed end is at the left and the open end is at the right.
The displacement pattern from left to right is
opt_a: antinode at the closed end and node at the open end
opt_b: node at the closed end and antinode at the open end
explanation: The closed end of the air column does not allow air particles to move back and forth freely at the boundary. It is therefore a displacement node. The open end allows maximum particle displacement in the ideal boundary description, so it is a displacement antinode. In the fundamental mode, the pattern between them is the shortest node-to-antinode segment, equal to \(\frac{\lambda}{4}\). Pressure behaves oppositely, with pressure antinode at the closed end and pressure node near the open end. The displacement boundary conditions decide the shape of the air-column standing wave.
